deep.reconstruction:
This page contains no derivations. It is a run of dated claims from Gauss's scientific diary (the Tagebuch, published by Klein in 1903 and in Werke X.1). The year is 1800: the facing page has 1801 survey notes, and the next page has Nov 30 [1800] and Apr 6 [1801]. The entries correspond to Klein's numbers of roughly 105–113. Below, each entry is given with its modern mathematical content.

(1) Late May – Jun 2/3, 1800. The numerator and denominator of the lemniscatic sine, taken in the most general sense, are reduced to 'integral quantities'. In modern terms, Gauss writes sl(z) = M(z)/N(z) with M and N entire functions. M and N are given by everywhere-convergent products and series; in modern language they are theta functions attached to the square lattice Z[i]·ϖ, where ϖ = 2.62205755… is the lemniscate constant. At the same time he obtains infinite-series expansions of all lemniscatic functions 'from genuine principles', and calls this 'a most beautiful discovery, inferior to none of the preceding'.

(2) Same days. Principles for interpolating the arithmetic-geometric sequence. Take a_{n+1} = (a_n + b_n)/2 and b_{n+1} = sqrt(a_n b_n). Gauss extends the index n to an arbitrary rational value, so that the terms a_{p/q}, b_{p/q} are given by algebraic equations. In modern terms (my interpretation) this is the theory of modular equations / transformations of order n. The AGM step is the degree-2 (Landen/Gauss) transformation, and a rational index corresponds to transformations of other orders. In theta-function form this reads a_n = θ3(q^{2^n})^2 and b_n = θ4(q^{2^n})^2 (up to normalisation), with fractional n giving q^{2^{p/q}}.

(3) Jun 3, 1800, Braunschweig. Between two given numbers there are always infinitely many arithmetic-geometric and harmonic-geometric means, and Gauss has fully understood how they are connected. In modern terms this is the multivaluedness of the AGM for complex arguments. The sign choice of sqrt(a_n b_n) at each step yields a countable family of values μ. The reciprocals 1/μ form a lattice-like family: Gauss's later result is that any two values satisfy 1/μ' = d/μ + i c/λ, with λ = M(a+b, a−b), c ≡ 0 (mod 4) and d ≡ 1 (mod 4). The harmonic-geometric mean is HGM(a,b) = 1/AGM(1/a, 1/b) = ab/AGM(a,b).

(4) Jun 5. The theory is applied directly to general elliptic transcendents, i.e. elliptic integrals and functions of arbitrary modulus, beyond the lemniscatic case.

(5) Jun 10. The rectification of the ellipse is completed in three different ways. Likely candidates (my identification) are:
- the AGM formula L = (2π/M(a,b))·(a² − Σ_{n≥0} 2^{n−1} c_n²), with c_0² = a² − b²;
- the hypergeometric series L = π(a+b)·Σ binomial(1/2,n)² h^n, with h = ((a−b)/(a+b))² (the 'Gauss–Kummer' series);
- a Landen/transformation-based or theta series.

(6) Jun 12. 'A completely new numerical-exponential calculus.' The content is unknown. Klein's commentators guessed q-series / theta-type 'exponential' calculations; this is unsure.

(7) Oct 25. A problem from probability theory concerning continued fractions, earlier attempted in vain, is now solved. This is the Gauss–Kuzmin law. For x in [0,1] with continued-fraction expansion x = [0; a_1, a_2, …], let x_n be the n-th complete-quotient remainder. Then P(x_n < t) → log₂(1+t) as n → ∞, with invariant density 1/((1+t) ln 2) for the Gauss map T(x) = 1/x − ⌊1/x⌋.

No computation is shown on the page, so there is nothing to verify step by step.
errors: No mathematical errors can be assessed, since only claims are recorded. Gauss's own claim of a 'solution' to the continued-fraction problem was never published with proof; Kuzmin (1928) and Lévy (1929) supplied the first proofs.
The scribal crossings-out ('omnes', 'term', 'duo') are self-corrections and do not affect the content.

deep.surprise_reason: This is a page of Gauss's famous mathematical diary (entries c. 105–113, 1800). It has been published with commentary by Klein (1903) and in Werke X.1, and is extensively studied, e.g. by Gray and by Cox. All the results are already attributed to Gauss in the literature; the page records claims without new derivations.

checkable.asserts: The density 1/(1+x) is invariant under the Gauss map, i.e. the transfer-operator identity behind the Gauss–Kuzmin law. The sum telescopes as Σ(1/(k+x) − 1/(k+x+1)).
The Gauss measure is a probability measure on [0,1].
Lemniscate constant: ϖ/π = 1/M(1, √2), with ϖ = 2∫_0^1 dt/√(1−t⁴) = 2.62205755…; Gauss's AGM discovery underlying the page.
